title: Divisibility, mod, gcd & lcm
goal: Use `m | n`, `mod`, gcd and lcm correctly (including negatives and 0), trace both versions of Euclid's algorithm, and do Quiz-1-style one-line calculations.
magic: `n mod m` is always in `0 … m − 1` (so `−7 mod 3 = 2`).
gcd and lcm are always positive; `gcd · lcm = |m| · |n|`.
Slow Euclid: larger − smaller. Fast: `(m, n) → (n, m mod n)` until `(g, 0)`.

blocks.title: 💡 Learn it, one idea at a time
`m | n`: `n` is a whole-number multiple of `m`
blocks.summary: `m | n` means `n = k·m` for some integer `k`. It works for negatives and 0: everything divides 0, and 0 divides only 0.
blocks.picture: 12 cookies shared among 3 friends: everyone gets exactly 4, nothing left over. So `3 | 12`. Among 5 friends, 2 are left over, so `5 ∤ 12`.
blocks.official: For `m, n ∈ ℤ`, `m | n` ("`m` divides `n`", "`n` is divisible by `m`", "`n` is a multiple of `m`") is defined by `n = k · m` for some `k ∈ ℤ` (Week 1, slide 14). `m ∤ n` is its negation. For every `m`: `1 | m`, `−1 | m`, `m | m`, `m | −m`. `n | 0` for every `n`; `0 ∤ n` unless `n = 0`.

steps: `10 = k · (−3)` would need `k = −10/3`, not an integer: **no**.

trap.tempting: `m | n` means "`m` divided by `n`", a number.
trap.correct: `m | n` is a **statement** (true or false): "`m` divides `n`". The small number is on the **left**.
trap.test: Read it aloud as "`m` divides `n`". `3 | 12` is true; `12 | 3` is false.

blocks.magic: `m | n` ⇔ `n = k·m` for an integer `k`. `n | 0` always.

blocks.title: `n mod m`: the remainder, always between 0 and `m − 1`
blocks.summary: `n = k·m + r` with `0 ≤ r < m`. For negative `n` the remainder is still ≥ 0.
blocks.picture: A clock with 12 hours: 17 o'clock is 5 o'clock (17 mod 12 = 5). Going 7 hours **back** from midnight lands on 5 o'clock too: −7 mod 12 = 5.
blocks.official: `r = n mod m` is the remainder when `n` is divided by `m`, defined by `n = k · m + r` with `0 ≤ r < m` (Week 1, slide 14). **`m | n` if and only if `n mod m = 0`.** Warning for coders: Java/C `%` gives `−7 % 3 = −1`; the course's `mod` (like Python's `%`) gives `2`.

steps: We need `−7 = k · 3 + r` with `0 ≤ r < 3`.

tries.why: `5 = 0 · 8 + 5`. If `n < m` (and `n ≥ 0`), the remainder is `n` itself.

tries.q: `−12 mod 4`? What does that tell you?

trap.correct: The course requires `0 ≤ r < m`, so `−7 mod 3 = 2`.
trap.test: Check your remainder is in `0 … m − 1`. If it's negative, add `m`.

blocks.title: Primes, and numbers with nothing in common
blocks.summary: A prime is > 1 with divisors 1 and itself only. `m` and `n` are relatively prime when `gcd(m, n) = 1`.
blocks.picture: Primes are LEGO bricks that can't be split. Two numbers are coprime if they share no brick: 8 = 2·2·2 and 15 = 3·5 have nothing in common.
blocks.official: Numbers `> 1` divisible only by 1 and themselves are **prime**. Numbers `m, n` with `gcd(m, n) = 1` are **relatively prime** (Week 1, slide 15). Lecture exercise 1.2.12: two even integers are never relatively prime (2 divides both).

watch.q: Is 1 prime? Are 9 and 28 relatively prime?
steps: Primes must be `> 1`, so **1 is not prime**.
watch.answer: **1 is not prime. 9 and 28 are relatively prime** (neither of them is prime!).

tries.why: Neighbouring integers never share a divisor bigger than 1.

trap.tempting: Relatively prime means both numbers are prime.
trap.correct: It only means they share no divisor except 1. `8` and `9` are relatively prime; neither is prime.

blocks.magic: Prime: `> 1`, only 1 and itself. Relatively prime: `gcd = 1`.

blocks.title: gcd and lcm: always positive, and `gcd · lcm = |m| · |n|`
blocks.summary: gcd = biggest common divisor, lcm = smallest positive common multiple. Signs are ignored. `gcd(0, n) = |n|`; `gcd(0, 0)` is undefined.
blocks.picture: Two buses: one every 6 minutes, one every 10. They leave together again after `lcm(6, 10) = 30` minutes. The largest tile size that fits both a 6 m and a 10 m wall exactly is `gcd(6, 10) = 2` m.
blocks.official: `gcd(m, n)` and `lcm(m, n)` are **always taken as positive**, even if `m` or `n` is negative: `gcd(−4, 6) = gcd(4, −6) = gcd(−4, −6) = 2` (Week 1, slide 15). `gcd(0, 0)` is undefined; `gcd(0, n) = |n|` for `n ≠ 0` (slide 18). **Fact** (slide 16): `gcd(m, n) · lcm(m, n) = |m| · |n|`. Lecture exercise 1.2.9: for positive `m, n`, `lcm(m, n) = m·n` exactly when they're relatively prime, and `lcm(m, n) = n` exactly when `m | n`.

watch.q: Find `gcd(12, 18)` and use it to get `lcm(12, 18)`.

tries.why: `gcd(0, n) = |n|`: every integer divides 0, so the answer is the largest divisor of −9.

trap.correct: Only when `m` and `n` are relatively prime. In general `lcm = |m·n| / gcd`: `lcm(6, 10) = 60 / 2 = 30`.
trap.test: Check the gcd first. If it isn't 1, the product is too big.

blocks.title: Euclid's algorithm: subtract the smaller from the larger
blocks.summary: Replace the larger number by the difference until both are equal. That number is the gcd.
blocks.picture: Two ribbons, 21 cm and 15 cm. Cut the short length off the long one, again and again. When both pieces are equal, that length measures both ribbons exactly: it's the gcd.
blocks.official: Week 1, slide 19: `f(m, n) = m` if `m = n`; `f(m − n, n)` if `m > n`; `f(m, n − m)` if `m < n`. For `m, n > 0` it always terminates. It works because `gcd(m, n) = gcd(m − n, n)` for `m > n`: every common divisor of `m` and `n` divides `m − n`, and conversely. (The course's `euclid.python` program implements exactly this.)

tries.why: Always subtract the smaller from the larger.
Stop as soon as the two are equal.

tries.q: Why does `f` always stop for positive inputs? (The lecture's "Proof?")
tries.a: Each step replaces the larger number by a smaller **positive** number, so `m + n` strictly decreases but stays positive. A positive integer can't decrease forever, so the recursion ends.
tries.why: Termination argument: find a quantity that shrinks every step and can't go below a floor.

tries.q: Why does `d | m − n` and `d | n` give `d | m`? (The lecture's "why?")
tries.a: `m − n = a·d` and `n = b·d`, so `m = (m − n) + n = (a + b)·d`.
tries.why: Common divisors survive adding as well as subtracting.

trap.tempting: Subtract in a fixed direction, e.g. always `m − n`.
trap.correct: Subtract the **smaller from the larger**; otherwise numbers go negative and the algorithm breaks.
trap.test: After each step, both numbers must still be positive.

blocks.magic: Larger − smaller until equal. That common value is the gcd.

blocks.title: The fast version: jump straight to the remainder
blocks.summary: `gcd(m, n) = gcd(n, m mod n)`, stopping when the second number is 0.
blocks.picture: Instead of cutting 15 cm off a 100 cm ribbon six times, just ask what's left after cutting as many as fit: `100 mod 15 = 10`.
blocks.official: Problem set 1, Q7 introduces the faster version: `gcd(m, n)`: if `n = 0` return `m`, else return `gcd(n, m mod n)`. Taking `m mod n` does all the repeated subtractions of `n` in one step. (Q7 also asks you to adapt the correctness proof: try that yourself.)

tries.q: What happens if you start the fast version with the smaller number first, `(36, 84)`?
tries.a: One extra step: `36 mod 84 = 36`, so `(36, 84) → (84, 36)`, then as before → **12**.
tries.why: The first step just swaps them.

trap.tempting: Return `m mod n` as soon as it's small.
trap.correct: Keep going until the **second** number is 0; then return the first.
trap.test: Write every pair. The answer is the first number of the pair `(·, 0)`.

blocks.magic: `(m, n) → (n, m mod n)` until `(g, 0)`; answer `g`.

items.why: Subtract the smaller from the larger.

items.q: Trace the fast version on `(13, 8)`. How many steps?
items.why: Neighbouring Fibonacci numbers are the slowest case for Euclid.

blocks.sub: Quiz 1 style (a variation of Problem set 1, Q2(a)): gcd, lcm, mod, floor and ceiling in one line. Original numbers.

items.q: Why can two even integers never be relatively prime? (Lecture 1.2.12.)
items.a: **2 divides both, so their gcd is at least 2.**

items.q: Positive `m, n` with `gcd(m, n) = m`. What can you say?
items.why: `m` is a common divisor, so it divides `n`. (Conversely, if `m | n` then `gcd(m, n) = m`.)

check.expr: all((gcd(m, n) == m) == (n % m == 0) for m in range(1, 30) for n in range(1, 30))

items.q: Prove `gcd(2n + 1, n) = 1` for every positive integer `n`.
items.a: Let `d` be a positive common divisor. Then `d | 2n + 1` and `d | 2n`, so `d | (2n + 1) − 2n = 1`. So `d = 1`.

check.expr: all(gcd(2*n + 1, n) == 1 for n in range(1, 200))

items.a: **Every integer divides 0**, so the common divisors of 0 and 0 have no greatest element.
items.why: For `gcd(0, n)` with `n ≠ 0`, the divisors of `n` are bounded by `|n|`, so a greatest one exists.

items.q: `gcd(m, n) = 6` and `lcm(m, n) = 60` for positive `m < n`. Find every possible pair.
items.why: `m · n = 360`, both multiples of 6: `m = 6a, n = 6b` with `a · b = 10` and `gcd(a, b) = 1`: `(a, b) = (1, 10)` or `(2, 5)`.

check.expr: sorted((m, n) for m in range(1, 61) for n in range(m + 1, 61) if gcd(m, n) == 6 and lcm(m, n) == 60)

lines: `n mod m`: `n = km + r`, `0 ≤ r < m`. `m | n` ⇔ `n mod m = 0`.
Prime: `> 1`, divisors 1 and itself. Relatively prime: `gcd = 1`.
Euclid works because common divisors divide differences.
